issues.issue: The payment deadline reads "payable within $0 days after presentation by Lender of a statement," so the notice period is not legible from the text. When the increased-cost payment falls due cannot be determined.

This subsection converts a LIBOR Rate Loan to the Base Rate at the end of each Interest Period "unless Administrative Borrower properly has exercised the LIBOR Option," whereas Section 2.12(c) deems Borrower to have elected the LIBOR Option for every Interest Period unless it affirmatively opts for the Base Rate. The default position on rollover is stated twice, in opposite terms.

The deemed ongoing LIBOR election here is the mirror image of Section 2.12(a), which provides that the rate "automatically shall convert" to the Base Rate at the end of an Interest Period unless the LIBOR Option has been properly exercised. Absent any notice from Borrower, the two subsections produce different rates.

The subsection fixes obligations "under the provisions of this Section 2,15," but there is no Section 2.15 in the Agreement; the intended reference is Section 2.13. The clause that defines the scope of each Borrower's absolute liability points to nothing.

The waiver is framed entirely by reference to "Section 580(d) of the California Code of Civil Procedure," while Section 13(a) provides that the Agreement is governed and construed under New York law. Whether a New York-governed waiver of California antideficiency defenses operates as written is a live question.

Sub-clause (ii)(B) confers rights on "Agent and Lenders" — "Agent" is not a party to or defined term in this bilateral agreement, and "Lender" is singular throughout. The waiver is expressed in favour of persons who do not exist under this instrument.

The premium is imposed on any early termination "for any reason not set forth in Section 3.7(a)," including acceleration on default and sale of Collateral in an Insolvency Proceeding, and is justified by a recital of "impracticability and extreme difficulty of ascertaining the actual amount of damages." Whether that stipulation makes the charge enforceable liquidated damages rather than a penalty is the classic dispute this wording invites.

The grant reaches only "Borrower Collateral," whose definition enumerates no Real Property, yet Section 4.4(c) requires documents "to create and perfect Liens in favor of Lender in any owned Real Property acquired after the Closing Date" and Permitted Dispositions (g) contemplates releasing Real Estate Owned. Whether the granting clause itself reaches real property is unsettled.

The sequence is circular: Lender must return the note "when a Note Receivable ... is repaid in its entirety" but returns it "to facilitate its payment," and releases its Lien "promptly upon receipt of the final payment." Whether the note goes back before or after payoff is the very thing the sentence needs to settle.

The release duty is triggered when a note is "sold by Fund in accordance with the terms of this Agreement," which routes back through the Permitted Dispositions definition and its 80%-of-unpaid-balance sale limb. The content of the release obligation is only as determinate as that carve-out.

The representation measures the Borrowers' loan documents against forms "commensurate with forms and documentation used by prudent lenders in the same or similar circumstances," a benchmark that is nowhere defined. The sentence also makes the absolute claim that "all aspects of Borrowers' operations, comply with all applicable federal, state and local laws and regulations."
